findings.title: Email matching is case-sensitive, will miss blocked emails with different casing
findings.body: The `should_block?` method uses `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` which performs an exact string match. Since email addresses are case-insensitive (per RFC 5321, the local part is case-sensitive in theory but universally treated as case-insensitive in practice), a blocked email stored as 'Spam@Example.com' will not match a signup attempt with 'spam@example.com'. The email should be downcased before lookup, and ideally stored in a normalized (lowercased) form, consistent with how the User model handles emails.

findings.title: Validation has write side-effects: should_block? mutates match_count on every validation call
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count` and updates `last_match_at` in the database. This is called from a validator, meaning any call to `user.valid?` (not just `user.save`) will increment the counter. In the `UsersController#create` action, `user.valid?` is called explicitly on line 168 before `user.save` on line 172, so the match_count will be incremented twice for a single signup attempt. More broadly, any code path that calls `.valid?` or `.errors` on a user with a blocked email will produce spurious increments.

findings.title: Silent failure if record.save fails in should_block?
findings.body: If `record.save` returns false (e.g., due to a validation error or database issue), the method still returns the blocking decision based on the in-memory `record.action_type`. The match_count and last_match_at updates are silently lost. The return value of `save` should be checked or `save!` should be used, or at minimum the failure should be logged.

findings.title: Incomplete regex escaping in email_in_restriction_setting? allows regex injection via site settings
findings.body: The method only escapes dots with `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` before interpolating into a regex. Other regex metacharacters (e.g., `+`, `*`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{`, `}`, `|`, `^`, `$`) are not escaped. A malicious or mistaken admin could set `email_domains_whitelist` to something like `.*` or `(a{1,10000000})` causing either overly broad matching or a ReDoS attack. `Regexp.escape` should be used on each domain individually.

findings.title: Race condition in should_block? between read and write of match_count
findings.body: Under concurrent requests, two processes can read the same `match_count` value, both increment it in memory, and both save. One write will overwrite the other, resulting in a lost update. This is a minor data integrity issue for statistics, but could be fixed with an atomic `update_all` or `increment!` instead of read-modify-write.

findings.title: Email validator spec does not test whitelist/blacklist domain logic
findings.body: The spec only tests the blocked email path. The whitelist and blacklist domain checking logic (which was moved from user.rb) has no test coverage in this new spec file. Since this logic was refactored into a new class, it should have dedicated tests to ensure the behavior is preserved, especially edge cases around regex matching.
